# Broadcasting the Night {#sec-broadcasting}

Astrophotography live streams are their own small genre: the stacked
image climbing out of the noise while the numbers tick over beside it,
and a chat asking what scope that is. Polaris has everything needed to
be the source of one, and this chapter is about joining it up.

What makes it worth doing from Polaris rather than from OBS on a
laptop is what is missing from the picture. The usual way to stream a
session is to point capture software at a laptop screen, which means a
laptop at the scope, awake, plugged in, all night. Polaris broadcasts
from the host itself: the same small box already sitting on the
tripod, already doing the capture. Nothing else has to be there.

<!-- screenshot: the Live broadcast card in Settings, on air, with the
status pill and the uptime and bitrate line under the buttons -->

## What goes out

The host does not capture a screen. A headless box has no screen to
capture, and even where there is one, a browser window scaled to
1280x720 puts the image in the middle of a lot of sidebar. Instead
Polaris draws a frame of its own, laid out for someone watching on a
phone:

- Along the top, a **header**: the title you give the broadcast, the
  rig's name, and the equipment. Focal length and f-ratio, camera,
  mount, filter wheel, focuser, guide camera and guider, as far as
  they are configured. This is the answer to the question every astro
  chat asks, on screen from the first frame so nobody has to type it.
- On the right, an **object card**: a cutout of the target, its common
  name, its catalogue numbers, the facts (type, constellation,
  magnitude, apparent size) and a short description.
- Along the bottom, a **banner**: target, filter, exposure, gain,
  frames, total integration, SNR, guide RMS and sensor temperature.
- Everything else is the picture.

The split between the top strip and the bottom one is deliberate. The
header is fixed for the session; the banner is what changes. Someone
arriving in the middle reads the top once and the bottom continuously,
and mixing the two would make the part that is actually updating
harder to find.

Each of the three can be switched off, and the picture then has that
much more room.

## Where the picture comes from

Twice a second, Polaris asks for the best image available right now.
If a video stream is running, that is the picture, which is what you
want for planetary work. Otherwise it takes the last image the relay
handled, which covers LIVE, the stack, PREVIEW and AUTORUN, and which
the host keeps whether or not a browser is attached: you can close the
tab and the broadcast carries on. Failing both, it redraws the last
frame, so the picture holds steady between subs rather than going
black.

Two things it deliberately never does. It never starts a camera stream
of its own, because a stream holds the camera exclusively and would
block every exposure for as long as the broadcast ran. And it never
waits for an image. A two minute sub and a plate solve in the middle
of it are ordinary, and a broadcast that stopped sending during those
would stop every few minutes.

## Setting up a destination

Go to **Settings -> Network & security -> Live broadcast**, pick your
platform, and paste the ingest URL and the stream key that the
platform gives you.

| Platform | Where to find them |
|---|---|
| YouTube | Studio, Go live, Stream settings |
| Twitch | Creator Dashboard, Settings, Stream |
| Facebook | Live producer, Streaming software |
| Instagram | Live producer, on a professional account |
| Custom | any RTMP or RTMPS server, including your own |

Choosing a platform only fills the URL field in; what you save is what
is used. That matters for Twitch, which has regional ingest servers
worth choosing between, and for Instagram, which issues a fresh URL
and key for every session.

The commonest mistake is to paste the address of the studio page from
the browser's address bar instead of the ingest address. Polaris
recognises that and refuses it with an explanation, rather than
failing later with a connection error.

The stream key is treated as a credential, because it is one: anybody
holding it can broadcast to your channel as you. It is stored in its
own file on the host, readable only by the account Polaris runs as,
and it is never sent back to a browser. The field shows only whether a
key is set. Leave it untouched when you change something else and the
stored key is kept; clear it to remove the key.

## Quality, and what it costs

| Setting | Resolution | Bitrate | Per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 854x480 | 1000 kbps | about 0.5 GB |
| Medium | 1280x720 | 2500 kbps | about 1.1 GB |
| High | 1920x1080 | 4500 kbps | about 2.0 GB |

The per-hour figure is both the upload and, if you are recording, the
size on disk. Two things limit the sensible choice. The first is the
link: broadcasting from a phone hotspot in the field shares that link
with the browser session you are using to control the rig, and
starving your own control session to feed the stream is a bad trade.
Start at Low there. The second is the host, which the next section is
about.

## Recording, with or without an audience

**Also record to a file** keeps the same composed video as an MP4
under the capture folder. It works with a broadcast and it works
without one, and recording alone is a perfectly good use of the
feature: you get the timelapse of the night, with the card and the
numbers already burned in, and nothing goes anywhere near the
internet.

The file is written in fragments as it goes rather than being
finalised at the end. A night-long recording on a box that can lose
power is exactly the case where the usual arrangement fails badly: a
plain MP4 holds its index in memory until the writer exits, so a power
cut costs the whole file rather than the last few seconds.

## The object descriptions

The description on the card comes from one of three places, tried in
order. First the text Polaris ships, written for the Messier catalogue
and the better known NGC, IC and Sharpless objects. Then, if you have
left **Look up descriptions online** on and the host has a connection,
a description fetched once from Wikipedia in your interface language
and kept. Last, a sentence built from the catalogue facts, which is
mechanical but always correct and never absent.

That last one is why the card is never blank, and why the online
lookup can be treated as a bonus rather than a dependency. The
broadcast goes on air with whatever is already on disk; if a lookup
lands later, the card improves itself on the next frame. With no
network at all, nothing waits and nothing fails. A fetched text
carries a small credit line, which is not optional: it is published
under a licence that requires attribution, and a broadcast is
publishing.

## A second camera in the corner

The question every astrophotography chat asks after "what scope is that" is
"what does it look like out there". A small frame in the bottom left corner
answers it: an all sky camera, a camera pointed at the rig, or the guide frame.

Three sources, and the difference between them is what they cost.

**The guide camera** costs nothing. Polaris draws the frame the guide loop has
already taken, so no exposure is spent and nothing competes for the camera. It
needs the loop running, and it works with the built in guider only, because
PHD2 draws its own window and hands Polaris no pixels. What it shows is a
starfield at high magnification, which is interesting to an audience watching
guiding work and not at all a view of the sky.

**The auxiliary camera** also costs nothing, for the same reason: it is the
frame that camera's own capture loop took. Polaris never asks either camera for
an exposure of its own. It would have to queue behind that loop and behind your
focus snaps on the same capture gate, and three parties taking turns on one
camera is how a session stalls.

**A camera at a web address** is the one that answers the original question,
because an all sky camera is usually an IP camera rather than an astronomy one.
Give Polaris the address of a snapshot, the still image almost every such
camera serves, and it fetches one every few seconds. This costs nothing at the
telescope at all: no driver, no equipment slot, no contention. A stream address
(`rtsp://`) is not the same thing and will not work here; it wants a still.

Whichever you choose, give it a caption. Polaris has no way to know whether the
camera is pointed at the sky, at the mount or at the dog.

The corner never delays a frame. It draws whatever picture is already in hand,
and a source with nothing to show draws nothing rather than an empty box. When
a snapshot camera stops answering, the last picture stays up and the reason
appears under the buttons in Settings, where it is visible to you and not to
the audience.

One honest cost: the corner is more pixels to encode, and unlike the main
picture, which is unchanged between subs, it never stops moving. On a board
encoding in software that shows up in the bitrate and in the dropped frame
counter.

## What the host has to be able to do

Encoding H.264 is real work, and it happens next to the capture loop
all night.

Polaris needs `ffmpeg`, which the `.deb` recommends rather than
requires, so it may not be there. The card says so plainly, lists
every path it looked in, and offers to look again once you have run
`sudo apt install ffmpeg`.

Given ffmpeg, Polaris chooses an encoder by trying them. This is worth
a sentence because the obvious approach does not work: every ffmpeg
build advertises every encoder it was compiled with, and that says
nothing about whether the silicon behind one is present and usable.
A machine can list Intel Quick Sync, be chosen for it, and then answer
"could not open encoder" on the very first frame, which as a live
broadcast means a restart loop that never settles. So each candidate
is asked to encode a fifth of a second of black before it is trusted.
It costs about a second when you press Start.

On ARM boards the order is the Rockchip encoder (Orange Pi 5, Radxa),
then the kernel encoder most other boards expose, then software. On
x86 it is Quick Sync, NVENC, VAAPI, then software. The status line
tells you which was chosen and whether it is hardware.

If it is not hardware, be modest with the quality setting. A Pi 4
encoding 1080p in software while capturing and guiding will not keep
up, and the dropped-frame counter is where you will see it.

## While it is running

An **ON AIR** chip sits on the activity bar on every tab, so you can
work in FOCUS or LIVE and still know the broadcast is alive. It turns
amber the moment the encoder has had to be restarted.

Restarts are expected. RTMP connections drop, and from a hotspot at a
dark site that is an ordinary night rather than a fault. When the
encoder exits while you still want a broadcast, Polaris starts it
again with a backoff that tops out at thirty seconds, and counts the
reconnect. A slowly climbing count is the uplink; a fast one with an
error message beside it is worth reading.

**Stop** is a graceful stop. Polaris closes the encoder's input and
lets it finish, which is what puts the last fragment in the recording
and gives the platform a clean disconnect, and only kills the process
if it has not finished after ten seconds.

Nothing starts by itself. There is no scheduled broadcast and nothing
resumes after the host restarts. A broadcast puts your sky, your
equipment list and your session out under your own name, and it begins
when you press the button and at no other moment.

## What it does not do

- **No sound.** A silent audio track is sent because YouTube refuses a
  video-only stream, but there is no commentary: that would mean a
  microphone on the host, which is a different feature.
- **Instagram limits a session to about an hour.** That is Instagram.
- **Two frames a second reach the encoder.** For deep sky that is
  generous, since the picture changes once per sub. For planetary,
  where the video stream is running far faster, the broadcast is a
  slideshow of it rather than the stream itself.
- **Object types and constellation names stay in English**, because
  they come from the catalogue. The rest of the card follows your
  interface language.
